text:
A story on resettable fuses that an aerospace engineer once told me: GPS satelites have some of them. Now for ground testing, they use non-resetting fuses, which get swapped out for resettable ones prior to final assembly. After launch, the new satelites go through a series of tests to verify they are working correctly. One of these tests involved deliberately triggering the overcurrent protection. 

When they ran the test on one of two newly launched satelites, they suddenly lost contact with it. After a round of testing, debugging and analysis, they arrived at the conclusion that the fuses never had been swapped out, and the two satelites were launched with the test fuses still in place. 

Immagine the bone-chilling realization that there was another satelite in orbit with the same flaw, and ground control was about to begin the test sequence! A frantic phone call from the testing facility to ground control managed to get the test called off by mere seconds. 

So the second satelite had escaped doom by the skin of its metaphorical teeth. Bottom line is, one dead GPS satelite is orbiting earth, and another one has a damocles sword hanging over it, which is a very strange metaphor in microgravity. Oh and probably some GPS flight engineers and testers, when they have managed to entangle themselves in their bedsheets on a hot summer night, dream of that fuse getting hotter and hotter...

text:
Great video as always and a big +1 for Mouser!!! Two things to be aware of with PTCs vs a normal fuse or breaker though. The max interrupt rating and how fast it interrupts. PTCs are fine for low power electronics, but if there is a device with a high current source feeding it the PTC can destroy itself or not stop the inrush of fault current. Since, as like in your example, they can be rated as low as a 60 Amp interrupt rating. Fine for devices with small power supplies. But if you are powering something with a large power supply that can deliver 100's of amps (batteries, mains powered power supplies) and the device has a solid short the PTC may not be able to absorb the current spike. Whereas fuses have interrupt ratings from 5k up to 200k amps. Why some fuse holders are reject style holders, they will only fit a certain interrupt rated fuse and you physically can't install a lower rated fuse in the holder. 
Then there is the speed. Sure, tripping a 1A fuse or PTC with 2A will take a while, but how fast will a 1A PTC interrupt a fault with 20A of fault current vs a fuse that will instantaneously blow. 
Sure most of the viewers projects would be fine with a PTC, but to avoid possible damage with higher powered  devises a fuse or breaker is still needed. It can be in series with the PTC and at a higher trip level, yet will still provide protection in high current fault situations. PTC will take care of overloads and lower amperage faults and the fuse will take care of interrupting higher current faults that may have destroyed the PTC and NOT have interrupted the current flow.

text:
Polyfuses are great, and I agree they are an underappreciated and underused component. They're quite useful, simple and easy to integrate into designs, and very affordable. You do have to watch out for their quirks as noted in this video ("soft" trip, temperature dependence, don't quite reset to the same point after they've been tripped once) but any time you need overcurrent protection, they're worth considering as an option.

In most cases, I leave regular fuses for more "industrial" applications at higher currents especially where the chance of tripping them is very low unless somebody has done something seriously wrong. In the "electronics" space, if I have very tight thresholds for when to trip I'll use an e-fuse but otherwise the PPTC is my go-to for low current stuff.

Another related useful technique is the "crowbar" circuit. Basically, you use some mechanism to detect a fault condition in your circuit and then you deliberately short across the power rails to purposefully trip the fusing element. This can really expand your options for exactly what trips your fuse and can give you more precise control over the trip point while using a soft/simple trip element like a polyfuse, while still retaining the easy "unplug it for a bit to reset it" behaviour.

text: FWIW: In my designs I use a PTC & a TVS diode for overvoltage and reverse voltage protect. I put the TVS diode behind the PTC so if there is a overvoltage condition the PTC fuse will trip protecting the TVS diode. A unidirectional TVS diode can also protect against reverse polarity from the power source. TVS diodes (basically a Zener diode) will have a forward voltage drop of a bout 0.7V so it will limit reverse polarity to -0.7V. So with just two low cost components you get current protection, overvoltage protection, & reverse polarity protection.

text:
Not that good I would say, PTC fuses have at least 5 distinct drawbacks:
1. There is a peak current that must never be exceeded. For example a 1A Littlefuse RHEF100 has a maximum peak current of 40A. That means that in car applications, you must probably add an wire wound power resistor on the 12V supply line to keep the initial short circuit current within spec. 
2. PTC fuses wear out and degrade after approx 200 trip cycles. That means in practice that, if there is a permanent short circuit and the power of switched on and off (as in a car), or an intermittent fault, the PTC fuse may be worn out before you even realize there is a problem! 
3. Trip and hold currents are to a high degree temperature dependent. Does not work well over for example the -40 to +85C range usually required for automotive electronics. (RHEF100 goes from 1.36A to 0.56A trip current).
4. PTC fuses are not even considered as fuses in for example the EN 60950 safety standard. So if you're heading for a CE approval, the test house will apply a short circuit across the fuse during the safety testing! That's not much of a fuse then 🙄
5. Disc type PTC fuses are extremely slow compared to "F" melting fuses.. May be a problem if you want to protect sensitive semiconductors..
But If you can accept all the listed drawbacks, go for a PTC fuse 😁

These self resetting fuses are not Fuses. They are good for a limited number of cycles.The Best circuit protection is a good old mechanical circuit breaker. The only disadvantage is they are slow because current needs to rise above a set level.. Better than fuses and good for most circuits.
  Now for those who need lighting fast response. Remember that voltage drop leads current rise when a circuit fails.. On a should use a mechanical DPDT break before make type relay (or a Solid stare relay of you can fine one suitable) One pole is your on/ off switch  (normally off) and the other pole clamps open the load when power is removed.
The relay is controlled by a resettable JK FlipFlop. The flip flop is driven by a voltage detector If  the voltage drops below a preset level the circuit assumes there s a short and shuts down the load..
In the normally off mode it does consume power when the circuit is operating normally. 
In the Normally on mode  it does  NOT consume power when the circuit is operating normally. But a battery backup is recommended.
In the event of any failure the load is instantly separated from the power supply.
A failure would include a Brown out of the AC supply.
This circuit will work for a wide range of current capacities and depends on the relay specifications.
The trip point is precise.
Better than a crowbar circuit.
I use Mouser all the time, for decades.

text:
For some reason, all electronic build in China (and not designed by a Western Company) do lack a fuse, or any other type of protection. This is disgraceful.
I have been designing electronic systems for decades. I included a fuse of the proper size and speed on both sides of a power supply, i.e. on the main side (220 or 110 V) a slow-blow 2.5x max current, and a fuse on secondary, 3x fast blow type.
Resettable fuses (polyfuse) arrived on the scene in the '90s, and they were a godsend for inductive loads and generally for high power factor (cos φ < 0.68) devices. I begun using polyfuses in series with the primary of the main power supply transformers too, but I run into problems because the main transformer mode of failure: either the primary winding opens - no problem there; or the primary winding partially or fully shorts. The polyfuse intervene, heats up in few hundred milliseconds and presents a megaohm - level resistance. People plugged in and out the device, noting some reaction, and after few cycles, the polyfuse blew up: they can't be cycled quickly.
So I went back to slow-blow, sand-filled (arc damper) 5x20 fuses.
